assignment.title: Variables are labels
assignment.explain: A variable is a name pointing at a value. `=` means 'work out the right side, then stick this label on it'.
assignment.example:
score = 5
score = score + 1   # score is now 6
assignment.tip: Reading `x = x + 1` aloud as 'x becomes x plus one' helps.

tuple_swap.title: Swapping in one line
tuple_swap.explain: Python can assign several names at once. The whole right side is built first, so `a, b = b, a` swaps safely.
tuple_swap.example:
x, y = 1, 2
x, y = y, x   # x is 2, y is 1
tuple_swap.tip: In most languages you need a temp variable. Python doesn't!

augmented_assignment.title: Shortcut operators
augmented_assignment.explain: `x += 3` is short for `x = x + 3`. There are also `-=`, `*=`, `/=` and `//=`.
augmented_assignment.tip: Each line runs in order: keep a running value in your head.

indexing.title: Picking one character
indexing.explain: Strings are sequences. `s[i]` picks the character at position i, counting from 0.
indexing.tip: Index = how many steps from the start.

slicing.title: Slices
slicing.explain: `s[start:stop]` takes characters from start up to but NOT including stop.
slicing.tip: Length of a slice = stop - start.

string_methods.title: String methods & reversing
string_methods.explain: Methods like `.upper()` return a NEW string. `[::-1]` is a slice with step -1, which reverses.
string_methods.tip: Chained calls run left to right.

list_indexing.title: Negative indexes
list_indexing.explain: Lists start at index 0. Negative indexes count from the end: -1 is the last item.
list_indexing.tip: -1 is the easiest way to grab the last item.

list_methods.title: Changing a list
list_methods.explain: `append(x)` adds x to the end. `pop(i)` removes and returns the item at index i.
list_methods.tip: These methods change the list in place.

comprehensions.title: List comprehensions
comprehensions.explain: `[expr for item in seq if cond]` builds a new list: filter with `if`, then transform with `expr`.
comprehensions.example: [n * n for n in range(5) if n % 2 == 0]  # [0, 4, 16]
comprehensions.tip: Read it as a for loop squeezed into one line.

for_range.title: for loops & range
for_range.explain: `range(n)` produces 0 up to n-1. A for loop runs its body once for each value.

while_loop.title: while loops
while_loop.explain: A while loop repeats as long as its condition is True. The condition is checked before every turn.
while_loop.tip: Make sure something changes inside, or it loops forever!

nested_loops.title: Loops inside loops
nested_loops.explain: For every turn of the outer loop, the inner loop runs from start to finish.
nested_loops.tip: Total runs = outer count × inner count.

if_else.title: if / else
if_else.explain: `if` runs its block when the condition is True; otherwise the `else` block runs. Never both.
if_else.tip: Indentation shows which lines belong to each branch.

elif_chain.title: elif chains
elif_chain.explain: Python checks conditions top to bottom and runs only the FIRST one that's True.
elif_chain.tip: Order matters: put the strictest check first.

boolean_logic.title: and, or, not
boolean_logic.explain: `and` is True only if both sides are. `or` is True if either is. `not` flips. Priority: not, then and, then or.
boolean_logic.example:
True and False   # False
True or False    # True

return_values.title: Returning values
return_values.explain: `return` ends the function and sends a value back to the caller. Without it, a function returns None.
return_values.tip: print shows a value; return hands it back.

default_args.title: Default arguments
default_args.explain: Parameters can have defaults, used when the caller leaves that argument out.
default_args.example:
def greet(name, punct='!'):
    return 'Hi ' + name + punct

recursion.title: Recursion
recursion.explain: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller problem until it hits a base case that stops.
recursion.tip: Always find the base case first.

dict_basics.title: Dictionaries
dict_basics.explain: A dict maps keys to values. `d[key]` looks up the value.
dict_basics.tip: Keys are like labels on drawers.

dict_get.title: Safe lookups with .get
dict_get.explain: `d[key]` crashes with KeyError if the key is missing. `d.get(key, default)` returns the default instead.
dict_get.tip: Use .get when a key might not be there.

dict_loop.title: Looping over a dict
dict_loop.explain: `for key, value in d.items():` gives each pair, in the order they were added.
dict_loop.example:
for name, pts in scores.items():
    print(name, pts)
dict_loop.tip: Use .keys() or .values() if you only need one side.
